topics.title: 1. Computer Basics, Generations, Devices & Software
topics.theory:
- **Generations:** 1st = vacuum tubes (ENIAC = Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer, first all-electronic; **EDVAC = Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer**), **2nd = transistors**, 3rd = ICs, 4th = microprocessors (VLSI), 5th = AI/ULSI.
- **Parts of CPU:** ALU (arithmetic & logic), **Control Unit (the "nervous system" — directs and coordinates)**, registers; the CPU is the "brain" of the computer. Computer properties: speed, accuracy, diligence ("no I.Q." — works for hours without tiring), storage, versatility.
- **Input devices:** keyboard, mouse, **joystick**, scanner, **OMR (optical mark reader — reads answers to tests/surveys)**, **OCR** (text), barcode reader, MICR (cheques). **Output:** monitor, printer, plotter, speaker. **Impact printers:** **dot-matrix**, daisy-wheel, line printer; **non-impact:** inkjet, laser, thermal.
- **System software** (OS, compilers, assemblers, linkers, loaders, device drivers, utilities) vs **application software** (Tally = accounting, MS Office, browsers, DBMS applications). Batch file extension **.BAT**.
- **Information attributes:** accuracy, timeliness, relevance, completeness (isolation is not one). **Unicode** is the universal character set (UTF-8/16/32); **ASCII** is 7-bit (128 chars) / 8-bit extended, handles one language (English) or at most a few; characters have an assigned **collating sequence**. **Floating point numbers** = numbers with decimal point.
- **Memory units:** bit < byte < KB < MB < GB < TB < PB < EB < ZB < YB (each ×1024). **Supercomputer speed = FLOPS** (floating-point operations per second). **Embedded computers** use microcontrollers.
- **Privacy on social media:** avoid sharing personal info, check privacy settings.

qs.sol:
The arithmetic logic unit implements arithmetic such as addition and comparison as well as Boolean logic operations.

The control unit sequences instructions and the memory unit stores data, so the calculation and logic role belongs to the ALU.
qs.rel: ALU concept: arithmetic (add, subtract, compare) plus logic (AND, OR, NOT, XOR) and shifts. Neighbours: control unit directs but does not compute; flags (Z, C, S, V) are set by the ALU; accumulator is the usual ALU operand register.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an input device?
qs.sol: Joystick (Input Device): It is used to send signals to computers or gaming consoles (such as controlling movement in gaming).
qs.rel: Input vs output devices. Other inputs: light pen, trackball, touch screen, scanner, barcode reader. Outputs: plotter, printer, speaker, projector. Touch screen is both. Hard copy vs soft copy output is another common contrast.

qs.stem: Which generation of computer used transistor?
qs.sol:
The use of transistors marks the second generation of computers (roughly 1959–1965).

First generation computers used vacuum tubes; they were large and generated a lot of heat.

Second generation computers replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, making them smaller, faster, more reliable, and more energy-efficient.

Third generation computers used integrated circuits (ICs), and fourth generation computers use microprocessors.

Therefore, transistors were used in the second generation of computers.
qs.rel: Generation-technology mapping: 1st vacuum tubes, 2nd transistors, 3rd ICs, 4th microprocessor (VLSI), 5th AI/ULSI. Also expect programming language per generation: machine, assembly, high-level, 4GL, and the first microprocessor Intel 4004 (1971).

qs.stem: What is the file extension for Batch files?
qs.sol: Batch files in Windows operating systems use the .bat file extension. This standard format allows users to execute a series of commands sequentially as an executable script.
qs.rel: File extensions. .BAT = batch (list of commands run together), .EXE/.COM executable, .SYS system/driver, .DLL library, .TXT text. Know extensions of Word, Excel, PowerPoint (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) too.

qs.stem: Which of the following printer is type of impact printer?
qs.sol: A dot-matrix printer strikes an ink ribbon against paper, so it is an impact printer.
qs.rel: Impact vs non-impact printers. Impact: dot-matrix, daisy-wheel, line printer (strike ribbon, noisy, multipart forms). Non-impact: inkjet, laser, thermal. Speed units: cps, lpm, ppm; resolution in dpi.

qs.sol:
Concept: An arithmetic logic unit (ALU) is a combinational circuit that transforms operand values using selected arithmetic and bitwise operations. Comparisons may be implemented through subtraction, condition flags, or dedicated comparison logic.

The operation performed by a circuit and the purpose of its result are different ideas. An addition can produce either a numerical data result or an effective memory address; the processor design determines which circuit performs it.

Application: Consider a load using a base address of 1000 and a displacement of 12.

Read the base-register value, 1000, and the displacement, 12.

Add the two values: 1000 + 12 = 1012. …
qs.rel: ALU as combinational circuit: operations are selected by control signals; comparison is done by subtraction and flags. Related: ALU width equals word length; carry-lookahead speeds addition; ALU is part of CPU along with control unit and registers.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an impact printer?
qs.sol: Impact printers create images by physically striking an inked ribbon against paper. Dot-matrix printers function this way, whereas Inkjet and Laser printers use non-impact methods like spraying ink or fusing toner. Consequently, the dot-matrix printer is identified as the valid impact printer.
qs.rel: Impact printer identification. Dot-matrix forms characters from a pin matrix (9 or 24 pins); daisy-wheel prints fully formed characters. Laser uses drum, toner and heat; thermal uses heat-sensitive paper (receipts); inkjet sprays droplets.

qs.sol:
Concept

Printer classification depends on how marks reach the paper. An impact printer makes marks through mechanical strikes against an inked ribbon; a non-impact printer creates marks using ink deposition, electrostatic toner transfer, or heat without such strikes.

Physical contact alone does not define impact printing: rollers and heated print heads can touch paper without a striking mechanism.

Application

In a dot-matrix print head, selected pins move forward for each pattern of dots.

The pins strike an inked ribbon against the paper, transferring ink at the selected positions.

As the head moves, these dot patterns form characters. …
qs.rel: Printing mechanism decides impact vs non-impact class, not contact alone. Non-impact printers are quieter and faster but cannot make carbon copies. Expect questions on which printer prints in ppm (laser, inkjet) or needs toner (laser).

qs.stem: Which input device is used for reading answers to questions in a test or survey?
qs.sol:
Concept

Optical Mark Recognition (OMR) is an input technique in which a scanner detects the presence or absence of marks (filled bubbles, ticks or shaded boxes) placed at predetermined positions on a printed sheet. Because it senses the position of a mark rather than interpreting characters, it is the standard method for capturing responses on answer sheets, ballots and survey forms.

Application

In a test or survey, the candidate shades pre-printed bubbles for each chosen response. The OMR device shines light across the sheet and measures reflected intensity at each bubble location: a darkened bubble reflects less light and is registered as a selected answer. …
qs.rel: OMR reads pencil marks in boxes (exam answer sheets, surveys). Contrast: OCR recognises printed characters, MICR reads magnetic-ink cheque digits, barcode reader decodes bar patterns, biometric reader scans fingerprints.

qs.sol: The Intel 8085 has an 8-bit data path and is classified as an 8-bit microprocessor. Intel 8086 and Motorola 68000 are 16-bit families, while Intel 80386 is a 32-bit processor.
qs.rel: Microprocessor word sizes: 8085 is 8-bit, 8086 and 68000 are 16-bit, 80386 is 32-bit. 8085 has 16-bit address bus (64 KB). Data bus width, not address bus width, names the processor class.

qs.sol:
System software manages hardware resources, memory and devices, providing the base environment in which other programs run.

Application software is built for user activities such as writing, browsing or calculations; its purpose is task-specific.
qs.rel: System software manages hardware and runs other software: OS, compilers, assemblers, device drivers, utilities. Application software does user tasks. Also remember firmware (software in ROM) and language translators as system software.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not a key attribute of information?
qs.sol:
Good information is usually accurate, timely, and relevant. Accuracy means the information is correct, timeliness means it is available when required, and relevance means it is useful for the given purpose.

Isolation means separation and is not a standard key attribute of information quality.

Therefore, the correct answer is Isolation.
qs.rel: Attributes of good information: accurate, timely, relevant, complete, concise, understandable. Data = raw facts; information = processed data; knowledge = interpreted information. Isolation is not an attribute.

qs.stem: Due to which property a computer can work for hours without creating any error and without grumbling?
qs.sol: Diligence is the property of a computer by which it can perform tasks repeatedly for long hours without getting tired, bored, or complaining. Speed is about fast processing, and versatility is about doing different kinds of tasks. Therefore, the correct answer is Diligence.
qs.rel: Diligence is a computer property: no fatigue or loss of concentration. Other properties: speed, accuracy, versatility, storage capacity, automation. Disadvantages: no I.Q. (cannot think), no feelings, depends on instructions.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an example of System Software?
qs.sol:
Concept: System software supports the operation of a computer and the execution of programs. Language processors translate programs between representations, while application software performs tasks for users.

Classify software by its principal function rather than by whether other programs depend on it. A tool can be important to many applications without being a language processor or an operating system.

Consider compiling a small program that adds two integers. The compiler reads the source, checks its language rules, and translates it into target code, such as object code or an intermediate representation.

This translation helps prepare a program for execution. …
qs.rel: System software vs application software. Compiler, assembler, interpreter are language translators (system software). DBMS, word processor, browser are application software (some books class DBMS as system). Utility programs include antivirus and defragmenter.

qs.sol: Direct addressing puts the operand’s memory address explicitly in the instruction. The processor accesses that address to obtain the data.
qs.rel: Direct addressing: address field gives the operand's memory address, so EA = A and one memory reference is needed. Contrast immediate (no reference), indirect (two references), register indirect (one reference), relative and indexed.

qs.sol: A microprogrammed control unit reads microinstructions from control memory. Each microinstruction specifies control signals or sequencing needed to execute machine instructions.
qs.rel: Microprogrammed control unit keeps microinstructions in control memory (ROM). Contrast hardwired control (logic gates, faster, harder to change). Related: control address register, sequencer, horizontal and vertical microinstructions, CISC uses microprogramming.

qs.sol:
Concept: A processor separates the program it executes from the internal control steps that implement each machine instruction.

In a microprogrammed control unit, a control store (control memory) holds sequences of microinstructions. Each microinstruction specifies control signals and sequencing information for internal operations.

Application: Consider a machine instruction that adds a memory operand to a register. The following is an illustrative sequence; the exact steps depend on the processor.

The processor fetches and decodes the architectural ADD instruction from program memory. This instruction identifies the operation visible to software. …
qs.rel: Control store (control memory) holds the microprogram. Machine instruction opcode maps to a routine of microinstructions; writable control store allows microcode updates. Compare ROM-based control memory with hardwired decoding logic.

qs.stem: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) can only handle _____ or at most _____ languages and that shows its limitation to handle all world languages.
qs.sol: ASCII is a limited character-encoding standard primarily suited to English. It can handle one or at most two language sets in this exam-style framing, unlike Unicode.
qs.rel: ASCII limitation: 7-bit, 128 characters, built for English. Unicode (UTF-8/16/32) supports all world scripts; extended ASCII is 8-bit with 256 characters; EBCDIC is IBM's 8-bit code. Collating sequence is the ordering of characters.

qs.stem: Assigned ordering among the characters used by the computer is known as ______.
qs.sol:
Concept: A collating sequence is the fixed ordering assigned to the characters of a character set (for example, ASCII), normally taken from each character's underlying numeric code. Whenever a computer compares two characters, or sorts a list of names or strings, it is really comparing those codes — so the collating sequence is what decides that 'A' comes before 'a', and that '2' comes before '9'.

Application: The stem describes exactly this idea — an assigned ordering among the characters a computer uses — which is the standard definition of a collating sequence. …
qs.rel: Collating sequence: fixed order of characters in a character set. In ASCII digits (48-57) come before uppercase (65-90) before lowercase (97-122), which affects sorting results.

qs.sol:
Answer: CPU — The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is called the brain of the computer because it executes instructions, performs calculations, and controls and coordinates all other hardware components.

CPU: Executes program instructions, performs processing, and manages hardware — hence the brain of the computer.

Control Unit (CU): A part of the CPU that directs operations and coordinates how instructions are carried out.

Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): A component inside the CPU that performs arithmetic and logical operations.

Visual Display Unit (VDU): The monitor that displays output; it does not process instructions.

Its arithmetic and control units are components of that processor, so the whole processor fits the analogy.

The CPU integrates these functions and manages the flow of information, making it the central control unit. Therefore, the correct answer is CPU. …

qs.stem: 1 Byte = ?
qs.sol: A byte is a unit of digital information that typically consists of 8 bits. A bit is the smallest unit of data in computing, representing a binary value of 0 or 1. In most computer systems, a byte is defined as 8 bits, which allows it to represent 256 different values (from 0 to 255). This standardization makes it easier to process and store data efficiently.

qs.stem: A collection of 4 bits is known as
qs.sol:
Correct answer: a collection of 4 bits is called a nibble.

Definition: A nibble is a group of 4 bits.

Why the other terms are incorrect:

BYTE — A byte equals 8 bits, so it does not match a 4-bit group.

WORD — The size of a word depends on the computer architecture (commonly 16 bits or 32 bits), not specifically 4 bits.

K.BYTE — A kilobyte represents about 1024 bytes (or 1000 bytes in decimal), which is far larger than 4 bits.

Mnemonic: 4 bits -> nibble; 8 bits -> byte.

qs.sol:

Answer: The operating system is not hardware.

Explanation: Hardware refers to the physical components of a computer that you can touch. Software refers to programs and operating systems that run on the hardware.

Keyboard — a physical input device; it is hardware.

Printer — a physical output device; it is hardware.

Operating System — system software that controls and manages hardware and provides services to applications; it is not hardware.

Mouse — a physical pointing/input device; it is hardware.

Therefore, the correct answer is the operating system because it is software, not a physical component.

opts.B: It is a hardware device used to intercept data
opts.C: It replicates itself and spreads automatically to other computers
opts.D: It misleads users by appearing as legitimate software while hiding its malicious intent

qs.sol:
A Trojan Horse malware is a type of malicious software that disguises itself as legitimate or useful software to trick users into installing it. Once installed, it performs harmful actions in the background without the user’s knowledge. It does not replicate itself like a virus or worm, nor does it necessarily lock files like ransomware. Its primary characteristic is deception—appearing safe while hiding malicious intent.

Correct answer: It misleads users by appearing as legitimate software while hiding its malicious intent.

qs.stem: 2³⁰ bytes and 2⁵⁰ bytes are respectively equal to ........ and ........ .

qs.stem: The maximum memory size of the third-generation Intel microprocessor (80286) is

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Concept: The maximum physical memory a processor can address is fixed by the width of its address bus. An n-bit address bus produces 2n distinct addresses; since each address points to one byte, the maximum addressable memory equals 2n bytes.

Application: In the 8086-family generation scheme (8086/8088 first, 80186/80188 second, 80286 third), the 80286 is the third-generation Intel microprocessor. Its address bus is 24 bits wide, so:

Address bus width n = 24 bits.

Number of addressable bytes = 224 = 16,777,216 bytes.

16,777,216 bytes = 16,777,216 / 1,048,576 = 16 MB.

Cross-check: A 20-bit bus (8086) gives 220 = 1 MB, and a 32-bit bus (80386) gives 232 = 4 GB. …

topics.deep:
- **Computer generations:**

| Gen | Period | Key technology | Software / examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1940-56 | **Vacuum tubes**, magnetic drum memory | Machine language; ENIAC, EDVAC, UNIVAC, EDSAC |
| 2nd | 1956-63 | **Transistors**, magnetic core memory | Assembly, FORTRAN, COBOL; IBM 1401/7090 |
| 3rd | 1964-71 | **Integrated circuits (SSI/MSI)**, semiconductor memory | OS, multiprogramming, high-level languages; IBM 360 |
| 4th | 1971 onwards | **Microprocessor (LSI/VLSI)**; Intel 4004 (1971) | PCs, GUI, networking, C/C++ |
| 5th | Present/future | **ULSI, AI**, parallel processing | Expert systems, natural-language, robotics |

- **Landmarks:** **ENIAC = Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer** (first general-purpose all-electronic computer); **EDVAC = Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer** (stored-program concept, von Neumann); EDSAC = first practical stored-program machine; Babbage = father of the computer (Analytical Engine); Ada Lovelace = first programmer; Pascaline = Pascal's calculator.
- **Classification by size/power:** **supercomputer** (weather, nuclear simulation; speed in **FLOPS**; PARAM in India), **mainframe** (banks, airlines, thousands of users), **minicomputer** (mid-size, multi-user), **microcomputer** (PC, laptop, tablet), **embedded** (microcontroller inside washing machine, car, ATM). By data handled: **analog** (continuous: thermometer, speedometer), **digital** (discrete 0/1), **hybrid** (ICU monitors, petrol pump).
- **Characteristics:** speed, accuracy, **diligence** (no tiredness), versatility, storage, automation, **no I.Q.** (does only what it is told), no feelings.
- **CPU parts:** **ALU** (add, subtract, compare, shift, AND/OR/NOT), **Control Unit** (the "nervous system": fetches, decodes, sends control signals, does no actual data processing), **registers** (fastest small storage). Von Neumann model = CPU + memory + I/O + one shared memory for program and data.
- **Input devices:** keyboard, mouse, trackball, **joystick**, light pen, touch screen, scanner, webcam, microphone, **barcode reader**, **OCR** (printed text to editable text), **OMR** (marks on answer sheets, surveys), **MICR** (magnetic-ink cheque numbers), biometric scanner. **Output:** monitor (CRT, LCD, LED), printer, plotter, speaker, projector.
- **Monitor terms:** pixel, resolution (e.g. 1920x1080), refresh rate (Hz), dot pitch, aspect ratio; **VRAM/frame buffer** stores the image, the display device (CRT/LCD panel) actually shows it; GPU computes it.
- **Printers:** **impact** = strike a ribbon (**dot-matrix, daisy-wheel, line, drum/chain**) - noisy, can make carbon copies; **non-impact** = **inkjet** (spray ink), **laser** (toner + drum, ppm), **thermal** (heat on special paper, receipts). Speed units: dot-matrix **cps**, line printer **lpm**, laser/inkjet **ppm**; quality **dpi**.
- **Software:** **system software** = OS, **language translators** (assembler, compiler, interpreter), linker, loader, device drivers, utilities. **Application software** = general (MS Office, browsers) or specific (**Tally** accounting, payroll). **Compiler** translates the whole program at once and lists errors together; **interpreter** line by line; **assembler** assembly to machine code. Firmware = software in ROM. Batch file = **.BAT** (also .CMD).
- **Common extensions:** .exe/.com executable, .txt text, .docx Word, .xlsx Excel, .pptx PowerPoint, .pdf, .html, .zip, .bat batch, .sys driver, .dll library.
- **Data vs information:** data = raw facts/figures/observations; **information = processed, organised, meaningful data**. Good information is **accurate, timely, relevant, complete, concise**; "isolation" is not an attribute. Knowledge = information + experience.
- **Character codes:** **ASCII** 7-bit = 128 characters (8-bit extended = 256); designed for English only. **EBCDIC** = 8-bit IBM. **Unicode** = universal code for all world scripts, forms **UTF-8** (variable 1-4 bytes, ASCII-compatible), UTF-16, UTF-32. ASCII values: '0' = 48, 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97 (so digits < uppercase < lowercase in the **collating sequence**).
- **Units:** 4 bits = nibble, 8 bits = byte; KB = 2^10 B, MB = 2^20, GB = 2^30, TB = 2^40, PB = 2^50, EB = 2^60, ZB = 2^70, YB = 2^80. Descending: Yotta > Zetta > Exa > Peta > Tera > Giga > Mega > Kilo.
- **Floating point numbers** are numbers with a fractional (decimal) point; integers have none.
- **Social media privacy:** share minimum personal data, use privacy settings, monitor children's sharing, avoid oversharing location, beware phishing and cyber-bullying. Excessive use harms attention and academics.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) match generation with technology or example machine; (2) microprocessor of the 4th generation / first microprocessor Intel 4004; (3) identify input vs output vs both (touch screen, modem); (4) MICR use in banking vs OCR vs OMR vs barcode; (5) which printer type is fastest/quietest/uses toner/cps vs ppm; (6) compiler vs interpreter vs assembler differences; (7) number of bits in ASCII, extended ASCII, Unicode UTF forms; (8) convert KB/MB/GB or order the units; (9) classify analog vs digital vs hybrid examples; (10) system vs application vs utility software examples such as antivirus, disk defragmenter.

topics.title: 2. CPU Organisation, Registers, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
topics.theory:
- **CPU registers:** **PC/IP (Program Counter) holds the address of the next instruction**; **IR** holds the current instruction; **MAR** (address of memory location being accessed), **MDR/MBR** (data exchanged with memory); **AC (accumulator)**; **SP (stack pointer — holds address of stack top)**. I/O buffer register holds data being exchanged. **Instruction cycle** (fetch → decode → execute) = the processing for a single instruction.
- **Instruction format fields:** **opcode (operation to perform)**, **address field(s)**, **mode field** (addressing mode). Opcode with n bits → **2ⁿ operations**. **Mnemonics** = abbreviations for opcodes.
- **CPU organisations by address count:** **single-accumulator (one-address)** — implied AC (LOAD A: AC ← M[A]); **general register** (two-/three-address: ADD R1, A, B = three-address); **stack** (zero-address, PUSH/POP, postfix). Zero-address uses stack.
- **Addressing modes:** **Implied**, **Immediate (operand in the instruction)**, **Register** (operand in register), **Register indirect**, **Direct**, **Indirect** (2 memory references to fetch operand — 1 for address, 1 for operand), **Relative**, **Indexed (index register + address part)**, **Base register**, displacement mode EA = A + (R). **1 mode bit distinguishes direct vs indirect.** Register, immediate, implied modes do not need memory reference for operand.
- **RISC vs CISC:** RISC = few simple instructions, fixed-length, hardwired control, many registers, load/store, pipelining; CISC = many complex variable-length instructions, **microprogrammed control**.
- **Control unit:** hardwired vs **microprogrammed** (control memory with microinstructions; next-address generator = **microprogram sequencer**; some organisations need no decoder). Flynn: **MISD = Multiple Instruction stream, Single Data stream**, SISD, SIMD, MIMD. **Branch (BR ADR)** loads ADR into PC.

qs.stem: Which component is considered the 'brain' of the computer?
qs.sol: The central processing unit repeatedly fetches instructions, decodes them, and performs the required arithmetic or control actions. Because this execution and coordination role drives the rest of the computer, the CPU is described as its brain.
qs.rel: CPU is the brain: ALU + control unit + registers. Neighbours: memory is not part of CPU, control unit is the nervous system, ALU does computation. Clock speed in GHz and word size describe CPU capability.

qs.stem: Which of the following memory units communicates directly with the CPU?
qs.sol:
Main memory is directly addressable by the CPU for ordinary instruction and data access.

Secondary and tertiary stores require an I/O path.
qs.rel: Only main memory (and cache and registers) is directly accessed by CPU; secondary/auxiliary storage needs I/O operations. Memory hierarchy: registers, cache, main memory, disk, tape. Speed falls and capacity rises downward.

qs.stem: Which component of computer act as nervous system?
qs.sol:
To determine which component acts as the nervous system, consider the function of the nervous system: it coordinates and controls all body activities by sending signals.

Now evaluate each component:

Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): Performs calculations and logical operations. It does not coordinate or control other components.

Input Unit: Receives data from external sources. It does not manage or direct system operations.

Control Unit: Coordinates and directs all operations in the CPU. It sends control signals to other components to execute instructions.

Storage Unit: Holds data and instructions. It does not control or communicate with other components. …
qs.rel: Control unit fetches, decodes, and sends timing and control signals; it performs no actual data processing. Related: ALU computes, registers store, instruction register and program counter feed the control unit.

qs.stem: Which of the following registers of a CPU stores the address of the next instruction to be executed?
qs.sol: The Program Counter (PC) specifically stores the memory address of the next instruction to be executed by the CPU. Other registers like the Instruction Register hold current instructions, while the PC manages flow control. Thus, it is the correct register for this function.
qs.rel: Program Counter holds the address of next instruction and is incremented after fetch. Neighbours: IR holds current instruction, MAR address for memory access, MDR data, SP stack top. Branch instructions overwrite PC.

qs.stem: What is the function of the program counter register?

opts.B: It holds the address of current instruction
opts.C: It holds the address of previous instruction
opts.D: It holds the address of next instruction

qs.sol: The program counter (PC) is a special register in the CPU that keeps track of the memory address of the next instruction to be executed. After fetching an instruction, the PC is updated to point to the subsequent instruction, enabling sequential execution of program code. This ensures the CPU knows where to fetch the next command in the program flow.
qs.rel: PC function: sequencing of instructions; changed by jump, call, return and interrupts. In the fetch cycle MAR <- PC, then PC <- PC + 1. Distinguish from IR (instruction) and MAR (any memory address).

qs.stem: What is the number of addressable units in a computer system, if memory addressing is at the byte level, and length of address bits is A?
qs.sol:
An A-bit address has two possible values per bit, giving 
2
𝐴
2
A
 distinct byte addresses.

Each address bit doubles the number of distinct addresses.
qs.rel: Address width arithmetic: A address bits give 2^A addressable units; capacity = 2^A x unit size. Neighbours: 10 bits = 1K, 16 bits = 64K, 20 bits = 1M, 32 bits = 4G locations.

qs.stem: How many memory references are required to fetch an operand in indirect addressing?
qs.sol: In indirect addressing, the instruction contains a memory address that points to the location of the operand. The first memory reference is used to fetch this address. The second memory reference is then used to fetch the actual operand from the address obtained in the first step. Therefore, two memory references are required.
qs.rel: Indirect addressing: first reference reads the pointer, second reads the operand (two references). Direct = one, immediate/register = zero. Multi-level indirection is possible but slower; useful for pointers and tables.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about components of CPU? 
(i) A CPU has only 2 components. 
(ii) Control Unit is a CPU’s component.
qs.sol: A Central Processing Unit typically contains three main functional units: the Control Unit, Arithmetic Logic Unit, and Registers. Statement (i) is incorrect because it claims there are only two components. Statement (ii) is correct as the Control Unit manages instruction execution within the processor structure.
qs.rel: CPU components: ALU, control unit and registers (three, not two). Some books describe CPU as control unit + datapath. Memory and I/O are outside the CPU in von Neumann model.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a common field found in instruction formats?
qs.sol:
An instruction format commonly has an opcode and may include an address and addressing-mode field.

A general sign field is not a standard common field.
qs.rel: Instruction format fields are opcode, address field(s) and mode field. Sign bit belongs to data representation, not format. Also instruction length, number of address fields, and register field vary by design.

qs.stem: Which of the following addressing modes stores the operand in the instruction?
qs.sol: Immediate addressing mode stores the operand directly within the instruction itself, embedding the data value in the code rather than referencing a memory address or register.
qs.rel: Immediate mode puts the operand in the instruction (no memory reference), useful for constants. Implied mode has operand implicit; register mode keeps it in a register. Direct needs one memory access.

qs.stem: Which of the following algorithms refers to displacement addressing mode?
qs.sol:
Displacement addressing forms the effective address by adding a displacement A to the contents of a register R: EA = A + (R).

The effective address sums a fixed displacement and register contents.
qs.rel: Displacement addressing: EA = A + (R). Relative uses PC, indexed uses index register, base-register uses base register. Direct EA = A, indirect EA = (A), register indirect EA = (R).

qs.stem:
To which of the following categories does the given instruction belong?

LOAD    A    AC←M[A]
A

One-Address Instructions

B

Two-Address Instructions

C

Three-Address Instructions

D

Zero-Address Instructions
qs.sol:
The instruction names one explicit memory address, A.

The accumulator AC is implicit in AC←M[A], so this is a one-address instruction.
qs.rel: Address-count classification: LOAD A has one explicit address with accumulator implicit (one-address). ADD R1,A,B is three-address; zero-address uses stack. Two-address forms like MOV R1,A overwrite one source.

qs.stem: Which of the following Instruction format use an implied accumulator (AC) register for all data manipulation?
qs.sol: One-address instructions commonly use an implied accumulator register for data manipulation.
qs.rel: Single-accumulator (one-address) organisation uses implied AC for ALU operations: LOAD, ADD, STORE. Contrast general-register (two or three address) and stack (zero address, PUSH/POP).

qs.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a RISC processor?
qs.sol:
Concept

An instruction set specifies the operations a processor can perform and how operands are represented. Simpler, regular operations reduce the work needed to decode and execute each instruction.

Pipelining overlaps stages of successive instructions. Instruction latency and the rate of completing instructions are different measures, so a design goal must be distinguished from a universal timing guarantee.

Application

RISC means Reduced Instruction Set Computer. Its classical design uses simple operations, regular instruction formats and relatively few addressing modes to keep the control logic simple. …
qs.rel: RISC characteristics: few simple fixed-length instructions, single-cycle execution, load/store architecture, many registers, hardwired control, pipelining. CISC has many instructions, variable length, many addressing modes.

qs.stem: Which of the following elements of a machine instruction specifies the operation to be performed?
qs.sol:
The operation code field specifies the action that the machine instruction performs.

The opcode identifies the operation to execute.
qs.rel: Elements of a machine instruction: opcode, source operand reference, result operand reference, next-instruction reference. Opcode of n bits gives 2^n operations. Mnemonic is the symbolic opcode name.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a correct statement about RAM?

opts.A: It stands for Read Access Memory.
opts.C: It can be directly accessed by the CPU.
opts.D: Its speed is greater than Cache memory.

qs.sol:
Concept

Random access means a memory location can be selected by its address without reading all preceding locations. Volatility describes whether stored data survives removal of power.

In the conventional computer memory hierarchy, the processor uses main memory for active programs and data, while cache holds nearby copies to reduce access time.

Application

A running program places its instructions and working data in main RAM. A load or store instruction identifies an address in that memory.

The CPU issues the memory request through the memory system. A cache hit may supply a load; on a miss, the requested data is fetched from main RAM through the memory controller. …
qs.rel: RAM: random access, volatile, directly accessible by CPU, read/write. SRAM is faster than DRAM. ROM is non-volatile. Do not confuse random access (constant time) with sequential and direct access.

qs.stem: In CPU, which of the following type of register is required by the control unit and contains the instruction currently being executed?
qs.sol: The instruction register holds the instruction currently being executed by the CPU control unit.
qs.rel: Instruction register holds the instruction being executed; the control unit decodes it. Neighbours: PC (next address), MAR (memory address), MDR (data), accumulator (ALU operand and result).

qs.stem:
State whether the following statements are true or false.

(i) With one-address instructions, the programmer generally has available only one general-purpose register, the accumulator.

(ii) Zero-address instructions are applicable to a special memory organization called a stack.
qs.sol: Statement (i) is true because one-address instructions implicitly use the accumulator as an operand, limiting available general-purpose registers. Statement (ii) is true because zero-address instructions operate on a stack where operands are implicitly accessed via push and pop operations without explicit memory addresses.
qs.rel: One-address machines have one accumulator; zero-address machines use a stack with implicit operands (postfix evaluation). Be ready to write code for (A+B)*(C+D) in 0-, 1-, 2- and 3-address forms.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about control unit?
 I. It manages and coordinate the entire computer system.
 II. It does not perform any actual processing  on data.
qs.sol:
Step 1: The control unit is responsible for managing and coordinating all components of the computer system, including the CPU, memory, and input/output devices. This makes statement I correct.

Step 2: The control unit does not perform actual data processing such as arithmetic or logical operations. These tasks are handled by the ALU. Therefore, statement II is also correct.

Step 3: Since both statements I and II are accurate descriptions of the control unit's functions, the correct choice is the one that includes both.
qs.rel: Control unit coordinates all components and performs no actual data processing. Neighbours: it generates control signals via hardwired logic or microprogram, uses clock for timing, and interprets the opcode.

qs.stem: Which of the following addressing modes does NOT store the operand in the memory?
qs.sol: Implied addressing defines the operand implicitly within the instruction or a specific register, avoiding memory access. In contrast, modes like Register Indirect and Memory Indirect require retrieving operands from main memory locations to function correctly.
qs.rel: Implied addressing has the operand built into the opcode (for example CMA, stack ops), so no memory operand. Register indirect, indirect and relative modes all reach memory. Immediate and register modes also avoid memory.

qs.stem: Which of the following are the three forms of memory typically, volatile and use semiconductor technology?
qs.sol:
Registers, main memory, and cache commonly use volatile semiconductor storage.

Secondary and auxiliary storage are generally nonvolatile.
qs.rel: Registers, cache and main memory are volatile semiconductor memories. Secondary storage (disk, tape) is magnetic/optical and non-volatile. Semiconductor non-volatile examples: ROM, flash, SSD.

qs.stem: In stack organisation of a CPU, the register that holds the address of stack is referred to as ____.
qs.sol:
The stack pointer register holds the address of the current top of the stack and changes on push and pop.

It stores the stack-top address.
qs.rel: Stack pointer holds the address of the stack top and is decremented/incremented on push/pop. Stack is LIFO; used for subroutine return addresses, interrupts, and postfix evaluation. Overflow and underflow are error conditions.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a CPU organisation type with respect to instruction formats?
qs.sol:
Accumulator, general-register and stack organisations are established CPU instruction organisations.

Queue organisation is not the usual CPU organisation in this classification.
qs.rel: CPU organisations by instruction format: single accumulator, general register, stack. Queue organisation is not one. Stack uses zero-address, accumulator one-address, general register two- or three-address.

qs.stem: Which of the following is defined as the memory address obtained from the computation dictated by a given addressing mode?
qs.sol:
An addressing mode specifies how the address field and register values are combined.

The resulting actual memory address is the effective address.
qs.rel: Effective address is the final operand address after applying the addressing mode (A, (A), PC + A, XR + A). Physical address after translation is a separate concept from virtual or logical address.

qs.stem: In which of the following type of addressing mode, the instruction specifies a register in the CPU whose contents give the address of the operand in memory?
qs.sol: In register indirect addressing, the instruction names a CPU register whose contents hold the memory address of the operand.
qs.rel: Register indirect: register holds the memory address of the operand, one memory reference. Compare indirect (memory location holds address, two references) and autoincrement variant used for stepping through arrays.

qs.stem: Machine instructions that involve movement of data in or out of registers and or memory locations belongs to which of the following categories?
qs.sol:
Data movement instructions transfer values between registers and memory or other locations.

Data movement covers transfers into or out of registers and memory.
qs.rel: Instruction categories: data movement (load, store, move, push, pop), data processing (arithmetic and logic), control (branch, call, halt), I/O. Data storage refers to memory, not an instruction class.

qs.stem: With reference to Operating System overview, which of the following defines the repertoire of machine language instructions that a computer can follow?
qs.sol:
The instruction set architecture specifies the machine-language instructions visible to software.

The ISA defines the machine-language operations a processor can execute.
qs.rel: Instruction set architecture is the machine-instruction repertoire visible to software; ABI and API are higher interfaces. Architecture (visible to programmer) vs organisation (hardware implementation) is the classic contrast.

qs.stem: Which field of instruction is used to locate the operands needed for an operation?
qs.sol:
The mode field specifies how the operand location is to be found from the instruction.

The official key selects Mode; an address field alone supplies a value whose interpretation depends on that mode.
qs.rel: Mode field says how to interpret the address field and locate operands; address field gives the address or value; opcode gives the operation. Relate to EA calculation and addressing modes.

qs.stem: In which of the following type of computers do the programs and data often reside in a different memory system?
qs.sol:
Many embedded computers use microcontrollers with separate program and data memories, an arrangement associated with Harvard architecture.

RISC and CISC describe instruction-set design, whereas stored-program describes storing instructions in memory.
qs.rel: Embedded computers often use microcontrollers with separate program memory (ROM/flash) and data memory (RAM), a Harvard-style arrangement. Von Neumann machines share one memory for code and data.

qs.stem: When computers are classified by their role within a larger device, which class commonly uses microcontrollers whose program instructions and runtime data reside in separate memory systems?
qs.sol:
Concept

Computer systems can organize instructions and data in two broad ways. A von Neumann organization uses a shared memory path, whereas a Harvard organization uses separate instruction and data memories or buses.

RISC and CISC classify instruction-set design; stored-program describes how executable instructions are retained. An application-oriented class instead groups computers by the purpose and setting in which they are used.

Application

The stem fixes the classification axis as the computers role within a larger device, then asks which role-based class commonly uses separate program and data memory systems. …
qs.rel: Harvard vs von Neumann architecture. Embedded microcontroller examples: washing machine, car ECU, remote. Harvard allows simultaneous instruction fetch and data access; von Neumann uses one bus and memory.

qs.stem: The CPU exchanges data with memory. For this purpose, which of the following registers specifies the address in memory for the next read or write?
qs.sol:
The memory address register holds the address for a pending memory read or write.

This register supplies the address for the next memory access.
qs.rel: MAR holds address for pending read/write; MBR/MDR holds the data transferred; PC next instruction; IR current instruction. Memory read: MAR <- address, control read, MDR <- data.

qs.stem:
Which of the given options best describes the truthfulness of the following statements?

i) A compiler translates the entire source code line by line.

ii) Computer architecture refers to those attributes of a system which are visible to a programmer.

iii) The Reduced Instruction Set Architecture (RISC) computer organisation reduces the cycles per instruction at the cost of the number of instructions per program to increase the CPU performance.

iv) All the arithmetic and logical processing is performed by the Arithmetic Logic Unit under the supervision of a control unit.
qs.sol:
Concept

A multi-statement true/false item is solved by judging each statement independently against its own governing definition or principle in computer organisation and architecture, and only then combining the four individual verdicts into one pattern to match against the options.

Application

Statement

	

Verdict

	

Reason




i

	

False

	

A compiler translates the source file into target code before execution begins; it does not translate and run the program line by line the way an interpreter does.




ii

	

True

	

Computer architecture covers the attributes of a system that are visible to a programmer, such as the instruction set, addressing modes, and data types. …
qs.rel: Mixed true/false on architecture: compiler translates the whole program (not line by line), architecture means programmer-visible attributes, RISC uses simple instructions and load/store. Judge each statement separately.

qs.stem: Which of the following part of the CPU has the necessary electronic circuitry to perform binary addition and shift operations in computer system?
qs.sol: The ALU performs arithmetic and logic operations, including binary addition and shift operations.
qs.rel: ALU performs addition and shifting using adders and shifters. Registers store, control unit controls, buses transfer. Related: barrel shifter, carry-lookahead, status flags.

qs.stem: The processing required for a single instruction execution by CPU is called _____.
qs.sol:
An instruction cycle comprises the CPU work needed to fetch and execute one instruction.

An instruction cycle spans the processing of one instruction.
qs.rel: Instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute (plus interrupt check). Machine cycle = memory/I/O access; clock cycle = shortest time unit. Pipelining overlaps instruction cycles.

qs.stem: What is the full form of MISD?

opts.A: Multiple Interrupt stream and Single Data stream
opts.B: Multiple Instruction stream and Single Data stream
opts.C: Many Interrupt stream and Single Digital stream
opts.D: Many Instruction stream and Single Digital stream

qs.sol:
Correct answer: Multiple Instruction stream and Single Data stream

In Flynn’s taxonomy, MISD expands as Multiple Instruction stream, Single Data stream. It describes an architecture where multiple instruction streams operate on the same data stream.

Final answer: Multiple Instruction stream and Single Data stream.
qs.rel: Flynn's taxonomy: SISD (uniprocessor), SIMD (vector, GPU), MISD (rare), MIMD (multiprocessor/multicomputer). Classification by instruction stream and data stream counts.

qs.stem: Which of the following is characteristic of a RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) processor?

opts.B: Instruction that manipulate operands in memory
opts.D: A large number (typically from 100 to 250) of instructions

qs.sol: RISC processors typically use fixed-length, easily decoded instruction formats and a simpler instruction set.
qs.rel: RISC features: fixed-length easily decoded format, hardwired control, load/store, large register file, single-cycle execution. Microprogrammed control and memory operands are CISC traits.

qs.stem: Which of the following in a microprogrammed control unit is a next address generator?
qs.sol:
The microprogram sequencer generates the address of the next microinstruction.

A control address register holds an address but does not generate it.
qs.rel: Microprogram sequencer generates the next microinstruction address (branch, increment, subroutine). Control address register holds the current address; control memory stores microinstructions; pipeline register holds output.

qs.stem: Which of the following microprogrammed control unit organisations does NOT need any decoder circuitry to generate the control signals?
qs.sol:
In horizontal microprogramming, individual control bits directly select control signals.

Thus there is no encoded control field that needs decoding.
qs.rel: Horizontal microcode has one bit per control signal (wide, fast, no decoder). Vertical microcode encodes fields and needs decoders (narrow, slower). Nanoprogramming is a two-level variant.

qs.stem: What happens when branch instruction “BR ADR” is executed?

opts.A: It transfers the value of ADR into IR.
opts.B: It transfers the value of ADR into AC.
opts.C: It transfers the value of ADR into PC.
opts.D: It transfers the value of ADR into MAR.

qs.sol: When the branch instruction BR ADR is executed, the address specified by ADR is loaded directly into the Program Counter (PC). This directs the CPU to fetch subsequent instructions from that new memory location, altering the program flow.
qs.rel: BR ADR is an unconditional branch: PC <- ADR. Conditional branches test flags. CALL saves PC on stack first, RET restores it. Branch targets can be absolute or PC-relative.

qs.stem: In an ideal microcomputer, where is the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) located?
qs.sol: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) is located inside the CPU. It performs arithmetic operations, such as addition and subtraction, and logical operations, such as comparison. Memory and I/O devices support the system but do not contain the ALU.

qs.stem: The basic architecture of computers was developed by:
qs.sol: The stored-program architecture, with program instructions and data held in memory for a processor, is associated with John von Neumann. The other people are associated with calculators, transistor scaling and early mechanical computers.

qs.stem: From the following options, identify the correct full form of ALU, which is a crucial component of the CPU in a computer system.
qs.sol:
PDF is a document format, not an audio format.
 WAV, FLAC, MP3 are audio file formats.

qs.stem: From the following options, identify the correct full form of ALU, which is a crucial component of the CPU in a computer system.
qs.sol:
Concept: In the standard CPU model taught here, the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) is the sub-component responsible for arithmetic operations (such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division) and logical/comparison operations (such as AND, OR, NOT, XOR, and relational comparisons) required by an instruction.

Application: Matching each option's wording to this definition, "Arithmetic & Logical Unit" is the only option that names the two operation classes (arithmetic and logical) that this component actually performs. "Automated", "Augmented", and "Advanced" each describe an unrelated quality (automation, enhancement, sophistication), not the arithmetic-and-logic function. …

qs.stem: All the calculations and decision making operations are performed in which unit?
qs.sol:
The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) is a major component of the CPU. It performs:

Arithmetic operations: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
Logical operations: Comparisons and logical decisions such as AND, OR, and NOT.

Since calculations and decision-making operations are handled by the ALU, the correct answer is:

qs.stem: Zero address instructions are necessarily used in _________ architecture.
qs.sol: In a stack machine the operands are implicit at the top of the stack. Therefore an arithmetic instruction needs no operand address field.

qs.stem: Zero address instructions are implemented with the help of
qs.sol:
Zero address instructions do not explicitly specify operands

Operands are implicitly taken from the stack

Used in stack-based architecture

qs.stem: What does the control unit generate to control other units?
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: “Row Facts” was corrected to “Raw facts,” and the information distractor was clarified to distinguish processed information from data. Data are raw facts or figures before interpretation or processing turns them into information.

qs.stem: What does the control unit generate to control other units?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
The CPU coordination unit issues electrical directives that select transfers and operations.

These directives synchronize the ALU, registers and memory during instruction execution.

qs.stem: What does the control unit generate to control other units?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: The control unit generates control signals to manage and coordinate the operations of other units in the CPU. These signals determine when and how components like the ALU, registers, and memory should perform their tasks. Control signals are essential for ensuring that data flows correctly and operations are executed in the right sequence. While timing signals help synchronize activities, control signals are the primary mechanism for directing other units. Therefore, the correct answer is control signals. …

qs.stem: The register that contains the address of the next instruction to be executed is called

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: The register that contains the address of the next instruction to be executed is the program counter. It keeps track of the memory address of the next instruction in the sequence. After each instruction is fetched and executed, the program counter is updated to point to the next instruction. This ensures the CPU executes instructions in the correct order.

qs.stem: To achieve parallelism, one needs a minimum of
qs.sol: Answer: 2 processors

qs.stem: Instruction format of machine level language consists of OPCODE and __________.
qs.sol:
A machine language instruction generally consists of:

Where:

Opcode (Operation Code): Specifies the operation to be performed (e.g., ADD, SUB, LOAD).
Operand: Specifies the data, register, or memory location on which the operation is performed.
Example:

Opcode = ADD
Operands = R1, R2

Therefore, the correct answer is:

Answer: B) Operand

qs.stem: The ALU of a computer responds to commands from the:
qs.sol:
Correct answer: Control Unit.

The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations, but it acts according to control signals. The Control Unit fetches and decodes instructions, then sends commands or control signals to the ALU and other CPU components.

Memory and input devices store or supply data; they do not directly command the ALU.

qs.stem: Which of the following is responsible for extending commands to Arithmetic Logic Unit of a computer ?
qs.sol: The control unit decodes instructions and directs operations of the ALU and other processor components.

qs.stem: Which of the following is the full form of CISC?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
CISC expands to Complex Instruction Set Computer.

It denotes a processor design with a rich instruction repertoire.

qs.stem: The register that contains the instruction that is being executed is called

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: In a computer system, different registers perform specific functions. The accumulator is used to store data for arithmetic and logic operations, not the instruction being executed. The program counter holds the memory address of the next instruction to be executed, not the instruction itself. The instruction register, however, is specifically designed to hold the instruction that is currently being executed. It stores the fetched instruction from memory so that the control unit can decode and execute it. Therefore, the register that contains the instruction being executed is the instruction register.

qs.stem: The operand itself is contained in an instruction of:
qs.sol: In Immediate Addressing Mode, the operand is contained directly within the instruction itself. For example, in 'ADD #5', the value 5 is embedded as part of the instruction. Other modes like Direct or Indirect addressing use memory addresses to locate data, rather than including the operand value within the instruction code.

qs.stem: A register in the microprocessor that keeps track of the answer or result of any arithmetic or logic operation is the ______.
qs.sol:
Concept: Registers are small, fast storage locations inside a processor. Data registers hold operands and intermediate results, while address registers locate instructions or stack entries.

In an accumulator-based processor, a designated data register receives arithmetic and logic results for later instructions.

Suppose the accumulator contains 5 and an addition instruction supplies 3. The arithmetic logic unit computes 5 + 3 = 8.

The operation writes 8 into the accumulator. A later operation can reuse this stored value as an operand.

The register retaining arithmetic or logic results in this conventional organization is therefore the accumulator. …

qs.stem: When a subroutine is called, the address of the instruction following the CALL instructions is stored in/on the
qs.sol: A date can be added to a document by typing it, inserting plain text, or inserting an updating date field. Therefore all listed methods are possible.

qs.stem: When a subroutine is called, the address of the instruction following the CALL instructions is stored in/on the
qs.sol:
When a subroutine is called, the processor needs to remember where to return after the subroutine finishes. This is done by storing the address of the next instruction (the return address) in a specific location.

The return address is typically pushed onto the stack, and the stack pointer is updated to point to the new top of the stack. After the subroutine completes, the return address is popped from the stack, and the program resumes execution from that address.

The Program Counter (PC) is responsible for holding the address of the next instruction to be executed. …
The oscillator produces regular clock pulses. Those timing signals coordinate state changes in the processor and other synchronous circuits, so operations occur in the intended sequence.
The IBM PC uses a 20-bit address bus, allowing it to address up to 1 MB of memory. Therefore, it uses 20 address lines, matching “20 Address lines.”

qs.stem: The part of the CPU that coordinates all the functionality of the computer and other components :
qs.sol: The control unit decodes instructions and directs operations among the processor, memory, and input/output units. The motherboard connects components, while the ALU performs arithmetic and logic.

qs.stem: The register which holds the address of location of memory to and from which data are to be transferred is known as

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Concept: A memory transfer carries two distinct pieces of information: an address selects a storage location, while data is the value stored at that location.

Processor registers have specialized roles: address selection, temporary data storage, and effective-address calculation are separate functions.

Application: Consider reading the value 27 from memory location 1000.

The processor places the address 1000 in the memory address register (MAR), identifying the location to access.

A read control signal requests the contents of that location; the returned value 27 enters the memory buffer register (MBR), also called the memory data register (MDR). …

qs.stem: What does the term "Harvard architecture" refer to in the context of microcontrollers?

opts.A: A type of microcontroller with high processing speed
opts.B: A microcontroller architecture that uses a separate memory space for instructions and data
opts.C: A microcontroller with advanced addressing modes
opts.D: A microcontroller with a large number of I/O ports

qs.sol:
Concept

A processor’s memory organization defines how it stores and transfers program instructions and data.

In Harvard architecture, instruction memory and data memory occupy separate address spaces, typically with separate buses. A von Neumann architecture instead uses a shared memory space and path.

Application

The description “a microcontroller architecture that uses a separate memory space for instructions and data” states this defining organization. The separation can allow an instruction fetch and a data access to occur at the same time, although actual speed still depends on the implementation. …

qs.stem: Which of the following architectures is suitable for a wide range of data types?
qs.sol:
Concept

An instruction-set architecture defines the data representations and operand sizes that its instructions can process.

An architecture is described as supporting a wide range of data types when the ISA specifies several integer widths together with additional numeric and packed-data formats, rather than merely naming a processor product.

Application

IA-32 is the 32-bit x86 ISA. Its documented programming model includes byte, word, doubleword, and quadword integer operands, x87 floating-point formats, BCD-related formats, and packed multimedia/SIMD data through MMX and SSE extensions. …

qs.stem: .......... of CPU is the place where actual execution of instructions takes place during data processing.
qs.sol:
The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the primary component of a computer that performs most of the processing inside a computer. It consists of several key parts that work together to execute instructions.

The Control Unit (CU) directs the flow of data and instructions within the processor. It manages the operation of the CPU but does not perform the actual arithmetic or logical calculations required for data processing.

The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) is specifically designed to perform arithmetic and logical operations on data. This component is where the actual execution of instructions involving data processing occurs within the central processing unit core. …

qs.stem: The most common addressing technique employed by a CPU is

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
The final BPSC key treats more than one of the named CPU addressing modes as applicable.

Direct, indirect, and immediate are established addressing modes; without a specified processor or workload, “most common” cannot rank them universally.

qs.stem: Which of the following is  not true  regarding  registers?

opts.B: Can hold either data or instruction

qs.sol:
Registers are internal CPU storage ✔

They can store data or instructions ✔

Registers are built using flip-flops ✔

The assertion “Registers cannot store intermediate results” is false ❌

The claim that registers cannot store intermediate results is false.

Answer: MOV is not a program control instruction.

Program control instructions change the flow of execution. Examples include JMP and CALL.

CMP compares operands and sets CPU flags. CMP itself does not transfer control but is commonly used before conditional jumps to influence branching.

MOV only transfers data between registers/memory and does not affect the program counter or control flow. Therefore MOV is not a program control instruction and is the correct answer.

qs.stem: Which microcontroller family is known for its widespread use in embedded systems, ranging from consumer electronics to industrial automation?
qs.sol:
Concept: An embedded system performs a dedicated control task inside a larger product. A microcontroller integrates a processor core, memory, and peripherals such as timers and input/output interfaces on one chip.

A processor core is the execution engine inside a chip; a microcontroller is the complete integrated device. Many manufacturers can use the same core family in different microcontroller products.

Application: Compare each named family by its role in a system.

In a washing-machine controller, a timer schedules sensor readings, the CPU runs the control program, and input/output interfaces drive actuators. These are typical embedded-control functions. …

qs.stem: The microcontroller used in many Arduino boards is based on which architecture?
qs.sol:
Concept: A development board contains a microcontroller; that chip has a processor core with an instruction-set architecture. The board name, chip model and architecture describe different levels of the hardware.

An instruction-set architecture specifies the operations and programmer-visible registers of a processor. Identify the chip first, then identify the architecture implemented by its core.

Application: The classic Arduino UNO R3 uses the ATmega328P. Arduino lists its CPU as AVR; the classic Nano and Mega 2560 also belong to the AVR-based board family.

Cross-check and contrast: Compare the processor families by their design and use. …

qs.sol: NOT, OR and AND return logical TRUE/FALSE values directly. IF can return different user-specified results, so it is the exception.

qs.stem: Which pair contains a computer architecture model and its implementation-level architecture, respectively?

The narrowed wording asks for a model followed by its implementation level. A stored-program model describes the computer organization; microarchitecture describes its concrete realization.

qs.stem: In IA-32 architecture along with the general flags, which of the following conditional flags is provided?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Concept: A processor flag is a bit that records a result or controls part of execution. In IA-32, EFLAGS separates arithmetic status flags, the string-direction control flag, and system flags or fields. A field can contain several bits, so a register entry is not necessarily a single flag.

Condition-code flags describe arithmetic outcomes; execution-control entries govern matters such as debugging, interrupts and I/O permissions. These categories must be distinguished before interpreting an exam’s terminology.

The arithmetic status group is CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF and OF. Conditional branches test combinations of these flags, such as ZF for equality.

TF is bit 8, the Trap Flag. …

qs.stem: In the fetch-decode-execute cycle, the contents of the Program Counter are first transferred to the :
qs.sol:
During fetch, the CPU copies the address in the program counter into the memory address register.

Memory is then read, and the fetched instruction reaches the instruction register through the data path.

qs.stem: The address ﬁeld of an instruction speciﬁes the address of a memory location that contains the address of the operand. What type of addressing mode is this?
qs.sol: The instruction points to a memory cell that holds the effective operand address. This extra address lookup defines indirect addressing.

The actions that implement the meaning of an instruction are actually carried out during instruction execution.
 An instruction goes through three main stages:
 Instruction Fetch – fetching the instruction from memory

Instruction Decode – decoding the instruction

Instruction Execution – performing the actual operation

Thus, the instruction’s meaning is implemented during the execution stage.

Answer: The CPU controls all other parts of the computer.

Explanation: The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the primary component that fetches, decodes, and executes instructions and coordinates the operation of all other hardware.

Control Unit (CU): coordinates and controls the CPU and the computer by fetching and decoding instructions and issuing control signals to memory, input, and output devices.

Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): performs arithmetic and logical operations on data as directed by instructions.

Registers: small, fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold instructions, data, and intermediate results during processing. …

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: The instruction ADD X Y names its operand locations directly in its address fields. No pointer dereference or index-register offset is specified; this is absolute (direct) addressing.

qs.stem: The instruction CMP R1, R2 compares the contents of registers R1 and R2 and updates the processor status flags accordingly. Which one of the following correctly identifies the hardware unit responsible for executing this instruction and the type of operation involved ?

opts.D:
Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU); arithmetic operation

E

CMP performs an arithmetic comparison, conceptually subtracting one operand from the other and setting status flags.

The ALU carries out that operation; the result need not be stored.

opts.D:
More than one of the above

None of the above

qs.sol: Concept: In IA-32 the 32-bit EFLAGS register is not one homogeneous set of bits. Intel groups its bits by the job they do: the status (condition-code) flags record the outcome of the last arithmetic or logical operation, a control flag steers string operations, and a further group of system flags and fields governs the execution environment - debugging, interrupt response and I/O privilege. A question of the form "which flags does the architecture provide alongside the general flags?" is therefore answered by reading off that further group, not by hunting for more result-recording bits. …

To find the clock period, use the formula:

Clock period = 1 / Clock frequency

Given: Clock frequency = 1250 million cycles per second = 1.25 × 10^9 Hz

Now calculate:

Clock period = 1 / (1.25 × 10^9) = 8 × 10^-10 seconds

Thus, the clock period is 8 × 10^-10 sec.
